summary: Lists requirements for supporting customer RSVP and RSVP-TE signaling over a BGP/MPLS IP-VPN. Customers want end-to-end quality of service, such as reserved bandwidth, across a provider network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A company wants to reserve a lane on a shared highway from one office to another, and this lists what the highway must do for that.

questions: how do you support qos over vpn
subtitle: Enabling end-to-end quality of service and traffic engineering across provider-shared networks.

tldr.problem: Internet service providers offering BGP/MPLS IP-VPNs to enterprise customers need those customers to receive guaranteed bandwidth and fast recovery for voice, video, and other time-sensitive services across the provider's backbone.
tldr.mechanism: Two models are possible: customers can use native RSVP signaling aggregated onto provider TE tunnels (C-RSVP), or end-to-end customer TE tunnels tunneled inside provider TE (C-TE LSP). The RFC lists requirements for both, including admission control, fast reroute, policy enforcement, and management.
tldr.outcome: Service providers have guidance on how to support QoS commitments across shared backbone networks while managing scalability, security, and operational complexity.

facts.label: Two main models
facts.value: C-RSVP path (native IP) and C-TE LSP (tunneled)

facts.label: RSVP state isolation
facts.value: Per customer; cascading failures from one customer must not affect others

today: RFC 5824 is an Informational RFC published in April 2010. It has not been obsoleted. The requirements describe what many service providers have deployed, often with vendor-specific solutions. The RFC intentionally does not specify a solution, allowing providers flexibility in implementation. Subsequent RFCs have addressed specific aspects, such as RSVP in Layer 3 VPNs. The document remains a reference for service providers designing VPN services with QoS guarantees.

sections.title: Quality of Service in Virtual Private Networks
sections.content:
Enterprise customers connected to BGP/MPLS IP-VPNs expect triple-play services: Internet access, telephony, and video. These services have different requirements. Voice requires low delay and jitter; video requires high bandwidth; data is flexible. When traffic crosses a provider's backbone, the provider must guarantee the quality the customer pays for. RFC 5824 describes requirements for enabling this.

The provider network uses MPLS-TE (Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering) Label Switched Paths (LSPs) between provider routers (P-TE LSPs) to manage bandwidth. A customer can send native RSVP signaling (C-RSVP) for individual flows that the provider aggregates onto these P-TE LSPs, or the customer can establish its own end-to-end TE tunnels (C-TE LSPs) across the provider backbone. Each model has trade-offs in scalability, control, and complexity. The RFC is informational: it defines what service providers need, not how to implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: A company connects two offices with a rental network. The company wants to reserve bandwidth for voice and video. The provider must plan how to do that without making the network too complex.

sections.title: Two Models: Customer RSVP Paths and Customer TE Tunnels
sections.content:
In the C-RSVP path model, a customer or customer equipment sends RSVP PATH and RESV messages (native IP packets) requesting a reserved flow from one site to another. A provider edge (PE) router receives these messages within a customer's VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) instance, aggregates the reservations from multiple customers or flows, and ensures a P-TE LSP with enough capacity exists. If the provider doesn't manage aggregation, the provider backbone must retain RSVP state for every customer flow, which scales poorly. The advantage is simplicity: the customer uses standard RSVP as if on a private network.

In the C-TE LSP model, the customer's equipment signals RSVP-TE PATH messages to establish end-to-end labeled tunnels (C-TE LSPs) across the provider backbone. These tunnels are independent; a PE must tunnel multiple C-TE LSPs into P-TE LSPs and manage constraints like bandwidth, priority, and affinity. The provider must support hierarchical LSPs (C-TE inside P-TE) or continuous LSPs where C-TE crosses P routers. The advantage is that the customer controls tunnels and can establish backups, request fast reroute, and select paths. The provider must manage more state and complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Model 1: The company sends reservation requests, and the provider bundles them. Model 2: The company sets up its own tunnels through the provider's backbone. Which one is simpler depends on the provider's network.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
Scenario I: Fast Recovery — A customer uses VoIP between two sites. It establishes two C-TE LSPs: a primary path and a backup path through different provider routers. If the primary link or PE fails, traffic switches to the backup in under 50 milliseconds (fast reroute), keeping the call alive. This requires end-to-end C-TE LSP support with FRR capabilities.

Scenario II: Strict QoS — A service provider operates its own network and rents from another provider. It establishes C-TE LSP1 with 100 Mbps for voice (priority 0) and C-TE LSP2 with 200 Mbps for video (priority 1). The provider's PE routers must select appropriate P-TE LSPs based on priority and available bandwidth. Preemption (high-priority traffic bumping low-priority) may be needed. Scenario III involves load-balancing voice and video across multiple customer sites with full-mesh C-TE LSPs. Scenarios IV and V show RSVP aggregation over P-TE LSPs and non-TE (LDP) LSPs, reducing the provider's state burden. Scenario VI combines non-TE backbones with customer-controlled C-TE LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: One customer needs fast failover for voice. Another needs strict bandwidth guarantees for video. A third wants its own private tunnels. A fourth trusts the provider and just uses the provider's aggregation.

sections.title: Requirements for C-TE LSPs and C-RSVP Paths
sections.content:
The RFC lists detailed requirements. For C-TE LSPs: providers must support selective P-TE LSP choice (picking LSPs by priority, affinity, class-type, or DSCP), graceful restart (traffic flows during PE restarts), rerouting (on link/node/SRLG failures or preemption), FRR (link, PE, and CE protection), and admission control (limiting C-TE LSPs and bandwidth per customer). Path Computation Elements (PCEs) should help compute paths. C-TE LSPs should be diversely routed across disjoint provider paths, optimized (shortest path under constraints), reoptimized with make-before-break, and support Diffserv-aware MPLS-TE for per-class-type resource allocation.

For C-RSVP paths: providers must support PE-CE admission control to limit RSVP messages and state per VRF, aggregation of C-RSVP onto P-TE LSPs (optionally with DS-TE), and transparency (RSVP messages unchanged in transit between customer sites). Both models require CE-PE routing (static, BGP, OSPF), scalability (minimize RSVP/RSVP-TE messages, state, and BGP churn), performance (low setup time, fast failure recovery), and management (MIB modules, diagnostic tools like traceroute).
sections.plainLanguage: The provider must let customers pick which backbone tunnel to use, handle network failures quickly, limit how many customer flows run at once, and make sure voice and video each get their own bandwidth guarantee.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The provider must not reveal its backbone topology to customers. It should limit RSVP control packets from untrusted customer routers to prevent denial-of-service attacks. If a customer router sends labeled packets, the provider edge must drop them if the label was not assigned by that PE on that link (label spoofing defense). Each customer's RSVP or RSVP-TE state must be isolated; flooding from one malicious customer must not affect others.

Operationally, backward compatibility is important: existing RSVP and MPLS-TE must continue to work. Complexity must not degrade network stability. Scalability is critical: every additional C-RSVP flow or C-TE LSP adds state, and thousands of flows across thousands of customers can overwhelm a provider's routers. The RFC recommends PCE use to offload computation from PE routers, and suggests aggregation (C-RSVP onto P-TE, C-TE onto non-TE LSPs) to reduce state. Performance must be evaluated: path optimality, LSP setup time, failure recovery time, and control plane overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Hide the provider's network from customers. Stop attacks. Do not let this crush the backbone with too many states to track. Make sure voice and video do not slow down the rest of the Internet.
